transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I'm here because... well, it's about these nights where I just eat. I sit there afterwards, and there are just crumbs and empty containers all around me. I always keep those plastic containers from the grocery store, you know, the ones the bakery uses for the muffins? My neighbor Shirley says I'm a hoarder for keeping them, but they're perfectly good for sending folks home with leftovers. Shirley's always got something to say, though, ever since she got that new vinyl fence put in and thinks she runs the neighborhood. 

But... oh, right. The eating. I sit there in the middle of all those empty containers, and I just feel so terribly ashamed. Just... disgusted with myself. It gets so bad that I can hardly even bring myself to pray. And then the next morning, I can barely look folks at church in the eye. I just feel so guilty standing there in the pews... I just can't keep living with this kind of shame.
Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during those nights?

Control? Oh, heavens, no. Not at all. Once I take that first bite after the house is quiet... it's like my good sense just steps aside. 

And speaking of quiet, it gets so incredibly still in my house these days. Well, except for that grandfather clock in the hallway. My late husband Arthur bought that clock at an estate sale back in '98. It chimes every quarter hour. Honestly, it used to drive me up the wall when he first brought it home, but now I kind of like the company. The man who sold it to Arthur swore up and down it belonged to a local judge, though I never believed that for a second. People will say anything to make a sale, you know? Just like that contractor who told Shirley her new vinyl fence would be completely "maintenance-free." Ha! I see her out there scrubbing it with a sponge and a bucket of soapy water every other Tuesday. 

But... oh, Lord, I'm sorry. You were asking about the eating. Yes. It's just... even while I'm sitting there, literally telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands just keep reaching for more. It's like I have no say in the matter at all.
Do you feel guilty right after you finish eating, or is it more after you've had time to think about it?

Oh, it's right away. The minute the eating stops, I just look around at all those crumbs and empty containers I mentioned before, and it hits me like a ton of bricks. 

Speaking of those containers, I actually have to sneak them out to the recycling bin at the crack of dawn now. If I don't, Shirley will see them. She's always peeking through her blinds. She thinks she's being subtle, but I can see the slats moving when I go out to get the morning paper. I actually mentioned her snooping to Pastor Miller—not the bakery boxes, heavens no, just the snooping—and he said we should just pray for her. Pastor Miller is such a sweet man. He's been with our congregation for fifteen years. His wife, Diane, makes the most wonderful ambrosia salad for the Sunday potlucks. She always uses the miniature marshmallows, the colorful ones, you know? 

But I'm getting off track, I'm sorry. You asked when the guilt happens. Yes, it's right then, sitting in the middle of the mess. The shame and disgust with myself is just instant. It's so heavy right in that very moment that I can't even bow my head to pray. And then, of course, that awful feeling just stays with me all night, which is exactly why I can barely look Pastor Miller or anyone else at church in the eye the next morning.
Do you enjoy the taste of the food while you're eating during those nights?

Taste it? Oh, heavens no. I don't even think I taste a thing. I'm usually just standing there right at the kitchen counter, and I eat so fast that I barely taste the pound cake or the crackers at all. Half the time, I catch myself swallowing before I've even rightly chewed! 

And speaking of that kitchen counter, I've been meaning to get the laminate redone for ages. Arthur put that faux-granite contact paper down back in 2005, and it's starting to peel terribly at the edges near the sink. I saw an advertisement in the Sunday paper for a handyman who does tile work. But you have to be so careful with handymen these days. Shirley hired a fellow off the internet to fix her gutters last fall, and he left his aluminum ladder right in the middle of her prize hydrangeas for three weeks! Crushed the poor blooms completely. She was furious, just marching up and down the property line complaining to anyone who would listen. But I suppose that's what you get when you don't check references, and I told her as much, though she didn't care to hear it. 

But... oh dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? You asked if I enjoy the food. No, I really don't. It just goes down too fast to even notice what it is I'm eating.
Are you usually eating during those nights because you're feeling upset or anxious about something?

Upset? Anxious? You know, I'm really not sure. I haven't really thought about it like that. I mean, I suppose everyone gets a little anxious now and then, but I couldn't say if that's what starts it all off. 

Though, speaking of being upset, you should have seen the state Shirley was in last Tuesday. The city came by to trim the oak trees near the power lines, and they just hacked away at the one in her front yard. Left it looking completely lopsided, like a bad haircut! She was out there waving her arms at the poor young man in the cherry picker. I felt a bit sorry for him, honestly. He looked no older than my nephew, David. David just started college over at the state university, studying business, if you can believe it. He used to be such a quiet little boy, always sitting in the corner with his building blocks while the other children ran around. His mother—my sister, Brenda—was always so worried he wouldn't make friends. But now he's in a fraternity and everything! Brenda practically burst her buttons telling me about it on the phone last week. 

But, oh my, listen to me rattle on. What were we talking about? Oh, right, if I'm upset when I eat. I honestly don't know if I am. I just... I haven't really noticed a connection like that. It just happens.
Do you think the eating happens when you're trying to distract yourself from feeling upset or anxious?

Distract myself? I... well, maybe? I don't really know. I've never really stopped to think if I'm trying to distract myself from anything. 

Speaking of distractions, though, you wouldn't believe the racket outside my window yesterday afternoon. The Johnsons three doors down decided to have their driveway repaved, and the noise from those machines was just unbelievable! It went on for hours. I tried to sit down and read my book—it's a lovely mystery novel Brenda lent me, set in a little village in England where everyone knows everyone else's business. Reminds me a bit of Shirley, actually! The detective in the book is a retired schoolteacher who knits while she solves murders. I used to knit, you know. I made a beautiful baby blanket for David when he was born, a pale yellow with little white ducks on it. Brenda kept it for years, even after he outgrew it. She said she couldn't bear to part with it because the yarn was so soft. I bought that yarn at a little shop downtown that closed back in... oh, it must have been 2012. The owner, Mrs. Higgins, moved to Florida to be closer to her grandchildren. Florida seems so humid to me, I don't know how people stand it. 

But I'm sorry, I'm wandering again, aren't I? You were asking if I eat to distract myself from being upset. I really couldn't say for sure. I just haven't paid enough attention to know if that's what's going on.
Do you think eating helps you feel better when you're feeling upset or anxious?

Feel better? Oh, I couldn't tell you. I'm usually in such a blur when it happens that I don't know if I feel better or worse or anything at all. 

You know what does make a person feel better, though? A nice, warm cup of chamomile tea. Brenda sent me a lovely tin of loose-leaf chamomile for my birthday last month. It came in this beautiful floral canister—violets, I think they were. Violets always remind me of my grandmother's house down in Georgia. She had this stunning violet wallpaper in her front hallway. It was velvet flocked, if you can imagine! You just don't see wallpaper like that anymore. Everything is so modern and gray these days. I was at the hardware store just Tuesday looking for a new knob for my pantry door, and all the paint swatches they had on display were just fifty different shades of gray and beige. It's so dreary. I told the young man working in the paint department—he had the most peculiar haircut, shaved completely bald on the sides and long on top—I told him people need more color in their homes! He just blinked at me and handed me my receipt. Young people today don't really know how to make conversation, do they? They're always just staring at those phones. 

But... oh goodness, there I go again. I'm so sorry, doctor. You asked if the eating makes me feel better. I honestly don't think I can say yes or no. I just don't pay enough attention to how I'm feeling when I'm standing there to know if it helps.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you've started during those nights?

Unable to stop? Well... yes. It's the strangest thing. Once I take that very first bite, usually after the house gets completely quiet, it's like my good sense just entirely steps aside. 

Speaking of the house being quiet, it really does get pin-drop silent around here at night. The only thing you can hear is that old grandfather clock out in the hallway. My late husband bought that clock at an estate sale over in Westover back in... oh, it must have been 1998. It has this deep, heavy ticking sound. It used to drive me absolutely up the wall when we first brought it home, kept me awake for weeks! But Arthur just loved it. He was always tinkering with old clocks and radios. He had a whole workbench out in the garage covered in tiny little screwdrivers and gears. I actually tried to clear that workbench off last spring, but I just couldn't bring myself to toss out his little plastic organizers. They're like the ones people use for sewing notions, you know, with all the little clear drawers? 

I used to sew quite a bit myself, actually. I made the most beautiful floral curtains for the guest room. But my hands just aren't what they used to be. The joints get so stiff these days, especially when it's going to rain. The weatherman on channel four said we're supposed to get a terrible storm this weekend, which reminds me I really need to bring my potted geraniums inside before the wind gets to them... 

Oh, dear me. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? You were asking if I can stop eating. Like I was saying... even though my hands get stiff during the day, when I'm standing there in the kitchen at night, I'll be in my own head telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' but my hands just keep reaching for more. I just can't seem to make them stop once I've started.
Do you usually think about or experience any strong emotions right before these episodes of eating happen?

Strong emotions right before? Gosh, I don't really think so. I don't remember feeling much of anything, just sort of... blank, I suppose. 

Blank... you know, that's exactly how my television screen looked on Tuesday morning. Just completely blank! I tried pressing the power button on the remote over and over, and nothing happened. It's one of those new smart TVs Brenda's husband got me for Christmas. I never asked for a smart TV, mind you. My old one worked just fine, the one with the built-in DVD player. I used to watch my old Doris Day movies on it. Oh, Doris Day had such a lovely singing voice, didn't she? 'Que Sera, Sera' is my absolute favorite. We used to sing that in the church choir back when Reverend Thomas was still around. He was such a wonderful man, always had a peppermint in his pocket for the children after Sunday school. Peppermints are so soothing for the stomach, aren't they? I buy those little individually wrapped ones from the pharmacy down on Elm Street. The pharmacist there, Gary, he just had his first grandchild, a little girl named Hazel. Hazel is such a classic name, it's making quite the comeback! My great-aunt was named Hazel, she made the most incredible peach cobbler every summer when the peaches were in season...

Oh, goodness gracious, I'm doing it again. I am so sorry, doctor. My mind just goes a mile a minute. You were asking if I have strong emotions before I start eating. Honestly, no, I don't think I do. I just haven't noticed any particular feelings or thoughts right before it happens.
Do you think something specific usually happens or you think something specific right before these episodes of eating start?

Something specific happening right before? No... no, I can't say that there is. It's usually just a normal evening. 

Just a normal evening, you know, like when I sit down to do my crossword puzzles. I get the daily paper delivered—well, the boy throws it in the bushes half the time, but I still get it. I love the Tuesday crosswords, they aren't quite as impossible as the Sunday ones. I was doing one just last night, and the clue was for a five-letter word for a type of wading bird. An egret! I knew it right away because my sister Margaret and I used to see them all the time when we went down to Florida. Margaret had this lovely little condo in Boca Raton. Oh, it was just beautiful, right on the water. She had this patio with white wicker furniture. You know, you have to be so careful with wicker outside, the humidity just ruins it if you don't treat it right. I told her to use that spray sealant, the kind they sell at the hardware store. The same hardware store where I saw that young man with the terrible haircut, actually. They really do have everything there. I bought a new watering can there last spring because my old plastic one cracked right down the side. It was green, my favorite color. Green always makes me think of the springtime when the daffodils first start poking up through the frost...

Oh, for heaven's sake. Listen to me prattling on about daffodils and wicker chairs! I'm so sorry, doctor. You asked if something specific happens right before the eating starts. No, nothing specific at all. I don't think any particular thought or event sets it off. It just... happens.
Do you feel like you're unable to control how much you eat during those nights?

Control how much I eat? Oh, no. Not at all. Like I was saying earlier, once I take that very first bite, usually after the house is completely quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside entirely. 

Good sense... you know, my mother always used to say I had more good sense than my brother Robert. Robert was always getting into scrapes. Once, he tried to climb the big oak tree in our front yard to rescue a stray cat, and he ended up getting stuck higher than the cat! The fire department had to come get him down. The fire chief, Mr. Henderson, was such a tall man. He used to organize the annual Fourth of July parade downtown. Oh, those parades were magnificent. They had marching bands, and floats, and the local Boy Scout troop would carry the flags. I remember one year, it rained so hard during the parade that the crepe paper on the floats melted everywhere. The streets were stained pink and blue for weeks! It looked like a giant box of watercolors had spilled all over Main Street. I used to love watercolor painting. I took a class at the community center back when Arthur was still working at the plant. The instructor, Mrs. Gable, she taught us how to paint landscapes. I painted a lovely picture of a lighthouse once, but the blue I used for the ocean was just a bit too bright...

Oh, goodness, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I am so sorry. You asked if I can control how much I eat. No, I really can't. Even while I'm standing there telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands just keep reaching for more. I just can't control it once I start.
Do you find that you're eating during those nights because the food doesn't taste good to you, or is it more that you just can't stop eating once you've started?

It's definitely not about the taste. Goodness, no. It's just like I was saying a moment ago, it's that feeling of... well, once I take that very first bite, usually after the house is completely quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside entirely. 

Speaking of the house being quiet, it's been so quiet since the neighbor's dog, Buster, went to live on a farm. Buster was a golden retriever, such a sweet boy, but he loved to bark at the mailman. Our mailman, Carl, he's been delivering on this route for twenty years. He always wears those little blue shorts, even in the dead of winter! I don't know how his knees don't freeze solid. Winter here can be so bitter. I remember the blizzard of '78, we were snowed in for three whole days. Arthur and I played so much gin rummy that I thought I'd go cross-eyed looking at the cards. I used to be quite good at cards. We had a bridge club that met every Thursday afternoon. Eleanor always brought her famous cucumber sandwiches. You have to slice the cucumbers paper-thin, you see, and use just a touch of dill in the cream cheese... 

Oh, dear, there I go again, off on another story! I apologize, doctor. You were asking if I eat because it doesn't taste good or because I can't stop. It's really that I just can't stop. Like I said, even while I'm standing right there in the kitchen, telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands just keep reaching for more. I just lose all control of it.
Do you think your eating episodes might be triggered by feeling lonely or empty since your husband passed away?

Well, lonely... I suppose so. But it's not just Arthur being gone, though I do miss him terribly. It really started getting this bad about five months ago. That's when my dearest friend, Martha, passed away. We played bridge together for years, and we always sat together at church. 

Church just hasn't been the same without her. We used to go to the early service, the 8:00 AM one, because Reverend Thomas always gave his best sermons then. He had such a booming voice, you didn't even need the microphone. He retired last year and moved to Arizona. Arizona! Can you imagine the heat? My cousin Betty lives in Scottsdale, and she says you can literally fry an egg on the sidewalk in July. I don't know why anyone would want to fry an egg on a sidewalk, really. It seems terribly unsanitary. Betty used to make the most wonderful deviled eggs for our family reunions, though. She put just a little pinch of paprika on top, and a tiny bit of sweet pickle relish mixed into the yolk. I tried to make them her way once for a church potluck, but I boiled the eggs too long and the yolks got that awful green ring around them. It's so embarrassing when you bring a dish to a potluck and nobody eats it. You just have to smile and pretend you don't notice...

Oh, for pity's sake, Belinda, stop rambling! I am so sorry, doctor. You asked about feeling lonely or empty. Yes, I suppose that's a big part of it. Like I said, this whole thing with the eating has been going on for about five months now, ever since I lost Martha. She was my closest friend at the bridge club and at church, and without her... well, things have just been very hard.
Do you think eating helps you cope with feeling lonely or empty since your husband and friend passed away?

Well, coping... I don't really know if I'd call it coping. I'm not sure if it helps with the empty feeling or not, to be honest. I just know that I do it. It's just something that happens when the house is so quiet. 

Quiet... it reminds me of the library downtown. I used to volunteer there on Tuesday mornings. The head librarian, Mrs. Higgins, was very strict about the noise level. She'd give you this look over her reading glasses if you even whispered too loudly. She had these beautiful tortoiseshell glasses, the kind they just don't make anymore. You know, you go to the eye doctor now, and all the frames are those thin wire things or bright plastic colors. I went to get my eyes checked last month, and the young man helping me tried to convince me to buy a pair of bright red frames! Can you imagine? Me, at my age, walking around looking like a stop sign. I told him, 'Young man, I am looking for something dignified, not something that belongs on a fire engine.' Fire engines used to be so much louder when I was a girl. Or maybe my hearing was just better then. My brother Robert always said I had ears like a bat, because I could hear him sneaking back into the house after curfew. He thought he was so clever, oiling the hinges on the back screen door, but he always forgot about the squeaky floorboard in the hallway...

Oh, my stars, I'm doing it again. I'm so sorry, doctor. You asked if the eating helps me cope with feeling lonely. I really don't know if it helps. I haven't really thought about it that way. I just know I feel so empty, and then I find myself in the kitchen. I'm just not sure.
Do you think eating makes the feeling of loneliness go away, even if it's just for a little while?

Well, go away... I don't think it really goes away. It's more like it just gets covered up for a few minutes, you know? While I'm eating, I'm just focused on the food, on chewing and swallowing. 

Swallowing reminds me, I need to pick up my thyroid medication from the pharmacy. They moved the pharmacy from the front of the store all the way to the back. It's terribly inconvenient now. You have to walk past all the seasonal aisles just to get your pills. Right now it's all Valentine's Day candy. Mountains of those little conversation hearts. Do you remember when they used to say things like "Be Mine" and "True Love"? Now they say things like "Text Me" and "BFF." I had to ask my granddaughter what BFF meant. Best Friends Forever, she told me. She's such a bright girl, my Sarah. She's studying to be a dental hygienist. She's always telling me I need to floss more. 'Grandma,' she says, 'you have to protect your gums!' She bought me one of those fancy electric toothbrushes for Christmas. It vibrates so intensely, it tickles my nose! It's like having a tiny jackhammer in your mouth. Arthur used to use a jackhammer when he worked for the city... 

Oh, goodness gracious, Belinda, reel it in! I'm so sorry, doctor. I just can't seem to keep my thoughts on a straight track today. You were asking if the eating makes the loneliness go away. No, not really. It doesn't make it go away at all. It's just a distraction, I suppose, but the empty feeling is still right there waiting for me when I'm done.
Do you feel like eating is something you have to do during those nights, or is it more like you're trying to fill a void?

Well, a void... I suppose it is a void, but it's more like I just can't stop myself once I start. It's the strangest thing. Once the house is quiet and I take that very first bite, it's like my good sense just steps aside completely. Even while I'm sitting there, literally telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now, you don't need this,' my hands just keep reaching for more. 

Reaching... it's like how my Arthur used to reach for the crossword puzzle every Sunday morning. He wouldn't even speak to me until he'd finished the across clues. He always used a pen, too. Never a pencil. He said using a pencil showed a lack of commitment. He bought these special blue ink pens from a little stationery shop downtown. The shop closed years ago, of course. Everything downtown is closing these days. They turned the old movie theater into a parking garage. A parking garage! We used to go to the pictures there for a quarter. I remember seeing 'Gone with the Wind' there when I was just a young girl. The velvet curtains were so grand, and they had a real organist who played before the film started. He wore a tuxedo with a red cummerbund. Red always was my mother's favorite color. She had this beautiful red wool coat she wore every winter... 

Oh, dear me, I've done it again, haven't I? I am so sorry, doctor. My mind is just wandering everywhere today. You were asking if I have to do it or if I'm filling a void. Like I was saying, it's just that I lose all control. I tell myself to stop, but I just can't seem to make my hands listen to my brain.
Do you feel like you're eating during those nights because you feel a strong urge to do so, or because you're trying to fill an empty feeling inside?

Well, an urge... I suppose it's an urge, but it's really just that I lose all control. Once the house gets so quiet and I take that very first bite, it's like my good sense just steps aside completely. Even while I'm sitting there, literally telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now, you really don't need this,' my hands just keep reaching for more. 

Reaching... it reminds me of how my Arthur used to reach for the crossword puzzle every Sunday morning. He wouldn't even speak to me until he'd finished the across clues. He always used a pen, too. Never a pencil. He said using a pencil showed a lack of commitment. He bought these special blue ink pens from a little stationery shop downtown. The shop closed years ago, of course. Everything downtown is closing these days. They turned the old movie theater into a parking garage. A parking garage! We used to go to the pictures there for a quarter. I remember seeing 'Gone with the Wind' there when I was just a young girl. The velvet curtains were so grand, and they had a real organist who played before the film started. He wore a tuxedo with a red cummerbund. Red always was my mother's favorite color. She had this beautiful red wool coat she wore every winter... 

Oh, dear me, I've done it again, haven't I? I am so sorry, doctor. My mind is just wandering everywhere today. You were asking about the urge or filling an empty feeling. Like I was saying, it's just that I lose all control. I tell myself to stop, but I just can't seem to make my hands listen to my brain.
Do you think the eating episodes started as a way to deal with the loneliness after your husband and friend passed away?

Well, yes, I suppose that's exactly what it is. It's been going on for about five months now, ever since my closest bridge partner and dear church friend died. 

Mary was her name. Oh, Mary was such a sharp bridge player. We played every Tuesday afternoon at the community center without fail. She always brought these little cucumber sandwiches with the crusts cut off. The crusts... you know, my Arthur absolutely despised crusts on his toast. Every single morning for forty years, I had to trim them off with a butter knife. We had this beautiful silver butter knife we received as a wedding present. It had a delicate little floral pattern on the handle. Peonies, I think they were. Or maybe carnations? Carnations are such a sturdy flower, aren't they? We actually had pink carnations at Mary's funeral. The funeral director was this terribly tall man who kept clearing his throat... just a little *ahem, ahem* every few minutes. He wore these black dress shoes that squeaked terribly on the linoleum down in the church basement. We used to have our Sunday school classes down in that basement when I was young. They painted it this dreadful shade of mustard yellow back in the eighties... 

Oh, for heaven's sake, Belinda, stop talking about the basement! I am so, so sorry, doctor. I'm doing it again, just talking your ear off about nothing. You asked when this started. Yes, it's been about five months. Losing Arthur was so hard, but when Mary passed away too, the house just got so unbearably quiet, and that's when all this eating started.
Do you feel like you're eating to fill an emptiness inside you or because you simply can't stop once you've started?

Well, emptiness... I suppose there is an emptiness, yes, but really, doctor, it's just that I simply can't stop. Like I mentioned before, once the house is perfectly quiet and I take that very first bite, it's as if my good sense completely leaves the room. I'm sitting there, literally saying out loud, 'Belinda, you have to stop this,' but my hands just have a mind of their own, reaching for more and more.

Speaking of hands... my grandmother had the most beautiful hands. So elegant, with these long, slender fingers. She used to play the piano for us every Christmas Eve. We had this old upright piano in the parlor, made of dark mahogany wood. The parlor always smelled of pine needles and peppermint during the holidays. We'd hang these delicate glass ornaments on the tree—the kind they just don't make anymore. Everything is plastic now, isn't it? I went to the department store last week to look for a new set of mixing bowls, and they were all just cheap plastic. The store was so crowded, too. People rushing about, not even saying 'excuse me' when they bump into your cart. I remember when shopping was an event, you know? Ladies wore hats and gloves... my mother had a lovely pair of white kid leather gloves...

Oh, good heavens, I'm rambling again, aren't I? I do apologize, doctor. My mind just flits from one thing to another like a butterfly today. But yes, to answer your question, it's not so much trying to fill an emptiness as it is just losing all control once I start eating. I just can't seem to make myself stop.
Do you think the eating happens because you're trying to fill the emptiness you feel since your husband and friend passed away?

Well, doctor, I know we were just talking about that, and I really wish I had a clearer answer for you. I suppose it could be the emptiness... it's just so hard to say for sure. I just know that once I take that first bite, the control is completely gone. But yes, the house is certainly empty now. Too empty, really. 

We used to have so much furniture to fill the space. We had this massive oak dining table that Arthur inherited from his great-aunt. It seated twelve people! Twelve! Can you imagine cooking for twelve people these days? The price of groceries is just scandalous now. I went to buy a simple roast last Tuesday, and the butcher—well, they don't even have real butchers at the supermarket anymore, do they? Just those young boys in the white aprons who don't know a chuck roast from a ribeye. Arthur used to go to a proper butcher shop every Saturday morning. They had actual sawdust on the floor to catch the drippings. It always smelled of cold meat and pine wood in there. Pine is such a distinct smell, isn't it? We had a huge pine tree in our front yard when we first bought the house, but it got struck by lightning back in ninety-three. Or was it ninety-four? The insurance adjuster had to come out, and he drove this terribly loud little orange car...

Oh, Belinda, for pity's sake. I am so sorry, doctor. I am just wasting your time today, going on and on like a broken record. You're trying to figure out about the emptiness, and here I am talking about sawdust and orange cars. To be perfectly honest with you, I'm just not sure if I'm eating to fill a void or not. I just know I can't seem to stop myself once I start.

Shirley's always got something to say, though, ever since she got that new vinyl fence put in and thinks she runs the neighborhood.

Well, yes, I suppose that's exactly what it is. It's been going on for about five months now, ever since my closest bridge partner and dear church friend died. 

Mary was her name. Oh, Mary was such a sharp bridge player. We played every Tuesday afternoon at the community center without fail. She always brought these little cucumber sandwiches with the crusts cut off. The crusts... you know, my Arthur absolutely despised crusts on his toast. Every single morning for forty years, I had to trim them off with a butter knife. We had this beautiful silver butter knife we received as a wedding present. It had a delicate little floral pattern on the handle. Peonies, I think they were. Or maybe carnations? Carnations are such a sturdy flower, aren't they? We actually had pink carnations at Mary's funeral. The funeral director was this terribly tall man who kept clearing his throat... just a little *ahem, ahem* every few minutes. He wore these black dress shoes that squeaked terribly on the linoleum down in the church basement. We used to have our Sunday school classes down in that basement when I was young. They painted it this dreadful shade of mustard yellow back in the eighties... 

Oh, for heaven's sake, Belinda, stop talking about the basement! I am so, so sorry, doctor. I'm doing it again, just talking your ear off about nothing. You asked when this started. Yes, it's been about five months. Losing Arthur was so hard, but when Mary passed away too, the house just got so unbearably quiet, and that's when all this eating started.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating episodes are a result of a lack of control or an attempt to fill an emotional void
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're eating to fill an emptiness inside you or because you simply can't stop once you've started?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I take the first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense steps aside, and even while I'm telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands keep reaching for more.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient eats because they cannot stop once they have started, which directly corresponds to the symptom of loss of control over eating.

patient.answer:
Well, emptiness... I suppose there is an emptiness, yes, but really, doctor, it's just that I simply can't stop. Like I mentioned before, once the house is perfectly quiet and I take that very first bite, it's as if my good sense completely leaves the room. I'm sitting there, literally saying out loud, 'Belinda, you have to stop this,' but my hands just have a mind of their own, reaching for more and more.

Speaking of hands... my grandmother had the most beautiful hands. So elegant, with these long, slender fingers. She used to play the piano for us every Christmas Eve. We had this old upright piano in the parlor, made of dark mahogany wood. The parlor always smelled of pine needles and peppermint during the holidays. We'd hang these delicate glass ornaments on the tree—the kind they just don't make anymore. Everything is plastic now, isn't it? I went to the department store last week to look for a new set of mixing bowls, and they were all just cheap plastic. The store was so crowded, too. People rushing about, not even saying 'excuse me' when they bump into your cart. I remember when shopping was an event, you know? Ladies wore hats and gloves... my mother had a lovely pair of white kid leather gloves...

Oh, good heavens, I'm rambling again, aren't I? I do apologize, doctor. My mind just flits from one thing to another like a butterfly today. But yes, to answer your question, it's not so much trying to fill an emptiness as it is just losing all control once I start eating. I just can't seem to make myself stop.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating episodes are a result of emotional eating due to loneliness
doctor.question: Do you think the eating happens because you're trying to fill the emptiness you feel since your husband and friend passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the psychological motivation (filling emptiness) for the binge eating, which is not a specific symptom in the patient's profile.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, I know we were just talking about that, and I really wish I had a clearer answer for you. I suppose it could be the emptiness... it's just so hard to say for sure. I just know that once I take that first bite, the control is completely gone. But yes, the house is certainly empty now. Too empty, really. 

We used to have so much furniture to fill the space. We had this massive oak dining table that Arthur inherited from his great-aunt. It seated twelve people! Twelve! Can you imagine cooking for twelve people these days? The price of groceries is just scandalous now. I went to buy a simple roast last Tuesday, and the butcher—well, they don't even have real butchers at the supermarket anymore, do they? Just those young boys in the white aprons who don't know a chuck roast from a ribeye. Arthur used to go to a proper butcher shop every Saturday morning. They had actual sawdust on the floor to catch the drippings. It always smelled of cold meat and pine wood in there. Pine is such a distinct smell, isn't it? We had a huge pine tree in our front yard when we first bought the house, but it got struck by lightning back in ninety-three. Or was it ninety-four? The insurance adjuster had to come out, and he drove this terribly loud little orange car...

Oh, Belinda, for pity's sake. I am so sorry, doctor. I am just wasting your time today, going on and on like a broken record. You're trying to figure out about the emptiness, and here I am talking about sawdust and orange cars. To be perfectly honest with you, I'm just not sure if I'm eating to fill a void or not. I just know I can't seem to stop myself once I start.
